description: TerraWise, a six-member team from Cairo, is building FieldShift Advisor: a web tool that turns NASA Earth data (temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, NDVI) into field-level crop guidance. It ranks crops and rotations under current, warmer, and drier scenarios using a transparent score checked against FAO guidelines, and shows results on an interactive map with Arabic/English summaries for farmers and extension workers.
summary:
TerraWise: smarter planting decisions with NASA data
Farmers today face a changing climate. The best time to plant is moving, and old habits no longer work. TerraWise helps farmers choose the right crop and the best planting window for their own field.
The farmer picks a location on the map, then chooses the crop, soil type, irrigation method, and what matters most to them (water saving, soil health, or stability). TerraWise compares this with more than 40 years of NASA climate data (NASA POWER, MODIS, and SMAP soil moisture). It then shows the best planting window, an irrigation calendar, and a "time machine" that shows how the ideal planting date has shifted over the years.
The farmer can send the result to an agronomist for review or download it as a PDF.
TerraWise turns satellite data into simple, local advice for every field.
details:
TerraWise — NASA Space Apps 2026

One line: TerraWise tells a farmer the best window to plant their crop, based on 45 years of NASA climate data for their exact field.

The problem

Climate change is moving the seasons. Heat waves arrive earlier and rain becomes less predictable, so the planting dates farmers have used for generations are less reliable. Small farmers usually have no easy way to check how the climate in their own field has changed.

How it works

Pick the field. The farmer searches for a place or drops a pin on the map. They can also draw the field boundary. The app checks that NASA POWER, MODIS, and SoilGrids data are ready for that location.

Configure the field. The farmer chooses:

the crop (wheat, maize/corn, rice, barley, sorghum, cotton, lentils, fava beans), marked as winter or summer crops

how the field is watered (rainfed, surface irrigation, drip, or well/groundwater)

soil type (clay, sandy, loam, silty), which is optional because the app can use SoilGrids satellite data if left blank

the month and week they usually plant

what matters most to them (water saving, soil health, yield stability), each rated 1 to 5

Get the result. The app calculates the best planting window and compares it with the farmer's usual date.

What the farmer sees

Best planting window. For example: "Best window to plant Barley this year: Nov 16 – Nov 29".

Year calendar. Each month is marked as safe, optimal, flowering (sensitive), heat risk, or frost risk. The farmer's usual planting date is shown on the same calendar.

Time machine. A slider from 2001 to 2050 shows how the best planting date moves with the climate. In the example, the date is 11 days later than in 2001, and a "Jump to 2050" button shows the future.

Irrigation window. It shows which weeks the crop needs irrigation, which weeks rain is usually enough, and which weeks are off season. It uses FAO-56 crop water requirements and NASA SMAP soil moisture.

Why this window. A short explanation, for example that flowering avoids the April heat waves and grain filling ends before the peak summer heat. It also shows the data source (NASA POWER, 1981–2025) and a confidence level.

Needs local review. The app is clear about what it cannot know: crop variety, field drainage, and local pest pressure.

Two views. There is a Farmer view and an Agronomist view. The farmer can send the result to an agronomist for review or download it as a PDF.

Data sources

NASA POWER (daily climate data)

NASA MODIS (satellite imagery)

NASA SMAP (soil moisture)

NASA GIBS (map layers)

SoilGrids (soil properties)

FAO-56 (crop water requirements)

Why it matters

It gives local advice for each field, not general advice for a whole region.

It shows the climate trend, not only today's answer.

It saves water by showing which weeks irrigation is really needed.

It keeps the agronomist in the loop and says plainly that it is timing guidance only.

Team

Belal Elnagar, Yara Mohamed, Omar Tarek, Marwa Mohamed, Mariam Wael, and Yasmine Medhat.
